explication:
1. This repository is a multi-surface product, not a single app. The main runtime pieces are:
   - `project/aitoearn-backend`: the primary cloud/backend monorepo
   - `project/aitoearn-web`: the Next.js marketing + product web app
   - `project/aitoearn-electron`: the desktop client, including its own bundled server
   - top-level Docker/Nginx assets for deployment and static hosting

2. The core backend is `project/aitoearn-backend`, organized as an Nx monorepo with two NestJS applications:
   - `aitoearn-server`: the main business API
   - `aitoearn-ai`: the AI/agent execution service
   Shared libraries provide cross-cutting infrastructure like MongoDB, Redis, queues, auth, assets, MCP, and SDK clients.

3. `aitoearn-server` is the central domain API. It owns the user-facing business modules for:
   - accounts and account groups
   - content/material/media management
   - platform connections and publishing
   - engagement and interaction workflows
   - credits, notifications, short links, tools, relay/OAuth, and internal/admin APIs
   It also renders a few server-side views for auth flows.

4. `aitoearn-ai` is the automation/agent side of the backend. It contains:
   - AI chat and task orchestration
   - image/video generation pipelines
   - draft generation
   - material adaptation
   - model/provider adapters for Gemini, Grok, OpenAI, and Volcengine
   - agent “skills” and MCP tool implementations
   This service is where long-running AI jobs, schedulers, and agent task handling live.

5. The main data flow in the backend is request-driven API plus background execution:
   - HTTP controllers accept commands from web/Electron/MCP clients
   - services persist state in MongoDB
   - Redis is used for pub/sub, task coordination, rate/state sharing, and locks
   - queue workers consume asynchronous jobs for publishing, engagement, credits, notifications, and AI media processing
   This separation is important: controllers are thin entry points, while work is pushed into queues/schedulers/consumers.

6. Persistence is mostly MongoDB, with a dedicated repository/schema layer in `libs/mongodb` and `libs/channel-db`.
   Those libraries centralize collection models such as users, accounts, publish records, media, notifications, credits, tasks, and interaction records.
   `libs/mongodb` appears to be the newer unified persistence layer for the main backend; `libs/channel-db` supports channel-specific task/account records.

7. External integrations are a major architectural boundary. The backend talks to:
   - social platform APIs for publishing and engagement: Douyin, Kuaishou/Kwai, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Twitter/X, Pinterest, LinkedIn, WeChat Official Accounts, Google Business
   - AI model providers: Gemini, Grok, OpenAI, Volcengine
   - object storage: Ali OSS and AWS S3 abstractions in shared libs
   - messaging/notifications: email, SMS, Feishu logging/alerts
   - optional relay OAuth service, used to avoid requiring every self-hosted deployment to register its own platform app credentials

8. The publishing subsystem in `aitoearn-server` is one of the biggest internal boundaries. It is split into:
   - high-level publish orchestration
   - platform-specific publisher implementations
   - staging/upload/media-container logic
   - webhook handlers for platform callbacks
   - schedulers that enqueue publish jobs
   - consumers that finalize publish state and update records
   This subsystem bridges content stored internally with platform-side credentials, media uploads, scheduled execution, and post-publish state tracking.

9. The engagement subsystem is separate from publishing, but similar in shape. It includes:
   - platform providers for comment/interaction actions
   - workers for distributing engagement tasks and replying to comments
   - record services for interaction history and reply logs
   - admin/internal APIs for task visibility
   This indicates the product treats “publish” and “engage” as distinct workflows, even though they target the same social platforms.

10. `aitoearn-ai` exposes APIs for user-facing AI features and agent execution. It includes:
    - content generation endpoints and logs
    - AI asset management
    - model configuration/pricing
    - task status schedulers
    - agent runtime and Claude-code router integration
    - MCP tool modules for media, subtitles, image/video editing, style transfer, drama recap, and utility actions
    The presence of MCP support means this service is designed to be called not only by the web app but also by external agents like Claude/Cursor/OpenClaw.

11. `project/aitoearn-web` is the main browser front end. It is a Next.js app with:
    - internationalized routes under `[lng]`
    - product pages for chat, draft box, accounts, brand promotion, tasks history, agent assets, and welcome/marketing content
    - a large component library for publish dialogs, chat, channel management, notifications, plugin onboarding, and account selection
    - client-side stores for user, agent, publish/plugin state, and caches
    It is the primary interactive UI that coordinates with the backend APIs and SSE/task streams.

12. The web app’s architecture reflects two usage modes:
    - marketing/public pages, SEO, and documentation content
    - authenticated product workflows for generating content, managing accounts, and launching publish/engagement tasks
    It also has explicit support for browser plugin flows and task/chat streaming, so the UI is built around live task state rather than simple form submission.

13. `project/aitoearn-electron` is a separate desktop product with a split architecture:
    - a React/Vite renderer UI
    - an Electron main process with modules for accounts, publish, reply, auto-run, tasks, tracing, tools, and platform integrations
    - a bundled server under `project/aitoearn-electron/server`
    The desktop app is not just a shell; it contains substantial automation logic and its own backend, likely for local workflows, plugin-style platform operations, and offline/sidecar features.

14. Deployment and operations are first-class in this repo:
    - `docker-compose.yml`, Nginx config, and Dockerfiles support self-hosted deployment
    - GitHub Actions run build/check/release workflows separately for backend and web
    - top-level `scripts` and backend `scripts/build-docker.mjs` support packaging
    - the backend README emphasizes API-key based usage, MCP endpoints, and optional relay configuration
    This suggests the architecture is intended for both SaaS hosting and private/self-hosted installations.

15. If you are drawing an architecture diagram, the clearest boundaries are:
    - clients: web app, Electron app, external MCP clients, browser/plugin flows
    - backend APIs: `aitoearn-server` for business workflows and `aitoearn-ai` for AI/agent execution
    - shared infrastructure: MongoDB, Redis, queues, object storage, email/SMS, platform APIs, AI providers
    - async workers/schedulers: publish, engagement, credits, notifications, AI task processing
    - optional relay/OAuth path for platform authorization in self-hosted deployments
